Monstera.title: Window light without scorch
Monstera.summary: Set up your Monstera near bright filtered light so new leaves can size up without burning.
Monstera.concept: Monsteras grow best with bright indirect light. Gentle morning sun can work, but harsh afternoon rays often scorch leaves.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Leaf Finder badge — build a calm indoor light routine.

quiz.prompt: What light setup is best for a Monstera starter in most homes?
options: Bright indirect light near a window
A dim corner far from windows

Monstera.title: Rotate for balanced growth
Monstera.summary: A quick weekly turn keeps your Monstera from leaning hard toward one side of the room.
Monstera.concept: Indoor plants chase the strongest light source. Rotating the pot helps the stem and leaves develop more evenly.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Balanced Canopy badge — train a fuller indoor silhouette.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Rotating a Monstera every week or two can help it grow more evenly.

Monstera.title: Water after the top dries
Monstera.summary: Monsteras prefer a soak-then-rest rhythm instead of staying wet all week.
Monstera.concept: Let the top layer of soil dry a bit before watering again. Constantly soggy soil raises the risk of root stress and yellowing.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Root Watch badge — protect roots from overwatering.

quiz.prompt: Your Monstera soil is still damp two centimeters down, but it is watering day on your calendar. What should you do?
options: Wait a bit longer and check again before watering
Water now because the schedule matters most
Add extra fertilizer instead of checking moisture

Monstera.title: Give climbing leaves support
Monstera.summary: A stake or moss pole helps mature Monstera growth feel purposeful instead of floppy.
Monstera.concept: Monsteras are natural climbers. Support can encourage larger leaves and a tidier growth habit as the plant matures.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Climber Coach badge — guide a stronger growth habit.

quiz.prompt: Why add support to a growing Monstera?
options: To keep the soil permanently wet
To replace the need for light

Monstera.title: Boost humidity the right way
Monstera.summary: Monsteras love moisture in the air, but misting alone is rarely enough.
Monstera.concept: Grouping plants together, using a pebble tray with water, or placing a small humidifier nearby raises ambient humidity more effectively than occasional misting.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Mist Master badge — create a consistently humid microclimate.

quiz.prompt: Which method raises humidity most reliably for a Monstera?
options: A pebble tray with water or a humidifier nearby
Moving the plant into full sun

Monstera.title: Choose a well-draining mix
Monstera.summary: Monstera roots need oxygen as much as they need moisture, so soil structure matters.
Monstera.concept: A chunky mix with perlite, orchid bark, or coir alongside potting soil keeps roots breathing between waterings and reduces rot risk.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Soil Scientist badge — build a breathable root zone.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Adding perlite or bark to potting soil helps Monstera roots stay healthier by improving drainage and airflow.

Monstera.title: Repot when roots need room
Monstera.summary: Moving your Monstera to a slightly larger pot at the right time prevents stress and supports growth.
Monstera.concept: Repot when you see roots circling the bottom or emerging from drainage holes. Choose a pot only one or two sizes larger — too much extra soil holds moisture and risks rot.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Root Room badge — give your plant the space it earns.

quiz.prompt: Roots are poking out of the drainage holes and growth has slowed. What is the right move?
options: Repot into a pot one size larger with fresh mix

Monstera.title: Wipe leaves to catch more light
Monstera.summary: A dusty leaf is an inefficient leaf — a quick wipe makes a real difference.
Monstera.concept: Dust blocks light from reaching the cells that power photosynthesis. Gently wiping leaves with a damp cloth every few weeks helps your Monstera run at full capacity.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Shine Keeper badge — maximize every ray of available light.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Wiping dust off Monstera leaves can improve the plant's ability to photosynthesize.

Monstera.title: Why Monstera leaves develop holes
Monstera.summary: Those famous splits and holes are a clever survival strategy, not damage.
Monstera.concept: In the wild, Monstera leaves develop holes and splits so wind and rain can pass through without snapping the leaf. Indoors this trait still appears as the plant matures under good light.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Fenestration Fan badge — appreciate the science behind the look.

quiz.prompt: Why do Monstera leaves develop holes and splits as the plant matures?
options: To let wind and rain pass through without tearing the leaf
Because the soil is too dry
Because the plant is getting too much water

Monstera.title: Work with aerial roots
Monstera.summary: Those thick roots growing from the stem are helpers, not problems.
Monstera.concept: Aerial roots absorb humidity and help the plant anchor itself as it climbs. You can gently guide them into the soil or a moss pole rather than cutting them off.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Aerial Anchor badge — use every root to your advantage.

quiz.prompt: What is the best way to handle Monstera aerial roots?
options: Guide them into soil or a moss pole
Never water the plant if they appear

Monstera.title: Ease off care in winter
Monstera.summary: Monsteras slow down when daylight shortens, and their care routine should slow down too.
Monstera.concept: Reduce watering frequency and stop fertilizing from late autumn through winter. The plant is resting, not struggling, and extra water or nutrients during this period can cause harm.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Winter Wisdom badge — match your care to the season.

quiz.prompt: True or false: It is safe to keep fertilizing a Monstera at full summer strength through winter.

Monstera.title: Spot and handle common pests
Monstera.summary: Catching spider mites or scale early keeps a small problem from becoming a big one.
Monstera.concept: Check the undersides of leaves regularly. Spider mites leave fine webbing; scale looks like tiny brown bumps on stems. Wipe affected areas with neem oil solution or insecticidal soap.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Pest Patrol badge — protect your plant before it suffers.

quiz.prompt: You notice fine webbing on the undersides of Monstera leaves. What is the most likely problem and first response?
options: Spider mites — wipe leaves with neem oil solution
Too much fertilizer — flush the soil with water

Monstera.title: Feed during the growing season
Monstera.summary: Monsteras push their biggest leaves when nutrients are available during spring and summer.
Monstera.concept: Use a balanced liquid fertilizer at half the recommended strength every two to four weeks from spring through early autumn. More is not better — over-fertilizing causes salt build-up and leaf burn.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Growth Fuel badge — time your feeding for maximum effect.

quiz.prompt: When is the best time to fertilize a Monstera?
options: Spring and summer every two to four weeks
Only in winter when growth slows

Monstera.title: Healthy roots, healthy plant
Monstera.summary: What happens underground directly controls what you see above.
Monstera.concept: Healthy roots are white or light tan and firm. Dark, mushy roots signal rot. If you spot rot during repotting, trim affected roots with clean scissors and let them air dry before placing in fresh soil.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Root Doctor badge — read your root system accurately.

quiz.prompt: What do healthy Monstera roots typically look and feel like?
options: White or light tan and firm

Monstera.title: Set realistic growth expectations
Monstera.summary: Monsteras are rewarding, but they grow on their own schedule indoors.
Monstera.concept: A Monstera in typical indoor conditions might push one new leaf every four to six weeks during the growing season. Bright indirect light, consistent watering, and seasonal fertilizing bring out the best pace.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Patience Pays badge — enjoy each new leaf as a milestone.

quiz.prompt: True or false: A healthy indoor Monstera typically produces a new leaf every four to six weeks during the growing season.

Monstera.title: Why soil drainage matters
Monstera.summary: Water-logged soil is one of the top causes of houseplant problems — drainage fixes this.
Monstera.concept: Soil that holds too much water starves roots of oxygen. A mix with good drainage materials like perlite or bark allows water to move through while still holding enough moisture for roots to absorb.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Drainage Detective badge — build a healthier root environment.

quiz.prompt: Why is good soil drainage important for most houseplants?
options: It prevents roots from sitting in water and losing oxygen
It makes plants grow faster in all conditions
It automatically prevents all pest problems

Monstera.title: Recognize overwatering early
Monstera.summary: Most houseplant problems trace back to too much water, not too little.
Monstera.concept: Signs of overwatering include yellowing lower leaves, a musty smell from the soil, and soft or mushy stems near the base. Letting soil dry out partially between waterings prevents most of these problems.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Overwater Spotter badge — catch this common mistake before it escalates.

quiz.prompt: Your plant's lower leaves are yellowing and the soil smells musty. What is the most likely cause?
options: Overwatering — let the soil dry out more between sessions
Too much light — move it to shade

Monstera.title: Read the signs of underwatering
Monstera.summary: Plants tell you when they are thirsty — you just need to know what to look for.
Monstera.concept: Drooping or wilting leaves that perk up after watering, dry soil pulling away from the pot edges, and crispy leaf tips are all signs that your plant needs water sooner.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Thirst Reader badge — respond before your plant shows real stress.

quiz.prompt: Which combination of signs most clearly points to underwatering?
options: Wilting leaves and bone-dry soil pulling from the pot edges
Yellowing lower leaves and very wet soil
Crispy tips and consistently moist soil

Monstera.title: Understanding indoor light levels
Monstera.summary: Not all bright spots are the same — the difference between bright indirect and low light is significant.
Monstera.concept: Bright indirect light means near a window but not in direct sun. Medium light is a few metres from a window. Low light is far from any window. Most foliage plants do best in bright indirect conditions.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Light Mapper badge — find the ideal spot in any room.

quiz.prompt: What does 'bright indirect light' mean for a houseplant?
options: Near a window but not in direct sun rays
In direct sun on a south-facing windowsill
In the middle of a room away from all windows

Monstera.title: NPK made simple
Monstera.summary: The three numbers on fertilizer labels tell you exactly what you are feeding your plant.
Monstera.concept: N is nitrogen for leaf and stem growth. P is phosphorus for roots and flowers. K is potassium for overall health and stress resistance. A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 suits most foliage plants during the growing season.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Nutrient Navigator badge — choose the right feed for every stage.

quiz.prompt: What does the N in NPK fertilizer stand for?
options: Nitrogen — supports leaf and stem growth

Monstera.title: Stem cutting basics
Monstera.summary: Propagating from a stem cutting is one of the simplest ways to multiply your plants for free.
Monstera.concept: Choose a healthy stem with at least one node (the bump where leaves and roots emerge). Cut cleanly below the node and place in water or moist soil. Roots typically emerge within two to four weeks.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Propagation Pioneer badge — grow your collection from what you already have.

quiz.prompt: True or false: A node must be present on a stem cutting for roots to develop successfully.

Monstera.title: Best time to repot any plant
Monstera.summary: Timing your repot well gives roots the best chance to settle quickly.
Monstera.concept: Spring is generally the best time to repot because plants are entering active growth and can recover quickly. Repotting in winter or during stress slows recovery and adds unnecessary strain.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Repot Timer badge — give your plant the best start in its new home.

quiz.prompt: When is generally the best time to repot most houseplants?
options: Winter, when the plant is resting
Any time the plant is currently flowering

Monstera.title: Decode yellowing leaves
Monstera.summary: Yellow leaves can mean several different things — the pattern tells you which one.
Monstera.concept: Yellow lower leaves often point to overwatering. Yellow upper leaves with green lower ones can suggest under-fertilizing or too little light. Yellow with crispy edges tends to mean underwatering or low humidity.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Yellow Detective badge — diagnose before you treat.

quiz.prompt: Only the lower, older leaves are turning yellow and the soil feels wet. What is most likely happening?
options: Too little light — move to a brighter spot

Monstera.title: Always use drainage holes
Monstera.summary: A pot without drainage is a gamble that most plants will eventually lose.
Monstera.concept: Without a hole at the bottom, excess water has nowhere to go and accumulates at the root zone. Even careful waterers struggle to avoid root rot in pots with no drainage. If you love a decorative pot without holes, use it as a sleeve over a plain nursery pot.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Drainage First badge — protect every root zone from stagnant water.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Growing plants in pots without drainage holes significantly raises the risk of root rot.

Monstera.title: Know when a plant is rootbound
Monstera.summary: A rootbound plant is sending a clear signal for more space.
Monstera.concept: When roots circle the bottom, crowd out of holes, or the plant dries out unusually fast after watering, it is rootbound. A one-size-up pot with fresh mix is the right response.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Space Giver badge — recognize the signal before growth stalls.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a clear sign that a plant is rootbound?
options: Roots growing out of drainage holes and the plant drying out very quickly
Leaves becoming very large and dark green

Monstera.title: Water thoroughly, then wait
Monstera.summary: A deep soak followed by a proper dry-out period beats frequent shallow watering.
Monstera.concept: Watering until water flows from the drainage hole ensures moisture reaches the full root system. Then waiting until the appropriate soil depth dries trains roots to grow deeper and builds drought tolerance.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Soak and Wait badge — master the single most impactful watering habit.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Watering until water drains from the bottom ensures the full root zone receives moisture.

Monstera.title: Simple ways to raise humidity
Monstera.summary: You do not need expensive equipment to keep humidity-loving plants happy.
Monstera.concept: Grouping plants together creates a local humidity bubble. A tray of pebbles and water placed under the pot adds gentle evaporation. A room humidifier near the plant is the most effective option for persistently dry environments.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Humidity Hacker badge — improve the air around your plant without breaking the budget.

quiz.prompt: Which of these methods most reliably raises humidity around indoor plants?
options: Using a pebble tray or humidifier near the plant
Spraying the top of the soil once a week
Placing the plant in a windowless bathroom

Monstera.title: Light changes with the seasons
Monstera.summary: The same window provides very different light in January versus July.
Monstera.concept: Sun angle changes throughout the year. A window that provides bright indirect light in summer may drop to medium or low light in winter as the sun tracks lower in the sky. Move light-hungry plants closer to windows in the colder months.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Season Tracker badge — adjust plant placement as light quality shifts.

quiz.prompt: True or false: A window that provides bright indirect light in summer may only offer medium or low light in winter.

Monstera.title: How plants signal stress
Monstera.summary: Plants cannot speak, but they communicate clearly if you know the signs.
Monstera.concept: Drooping signals thirst or heat stress. Yellowing leaves indicate watering or nutrient problems. Brown crispy edges often mean low humidity or overfertilizing. Pale or stretched growth points to insufficient light.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Plant Listener badge — respond to your plant's signals before problems escalate.

quiz.prompt: New growth on your Monstera is pale and stretching toward the window. What does this most likely mean?
options: The plant needs more light — move it closer to the window
The plant is too warm — move it to a cooler room
The plant is overwatered — let the soil dry completely

Monstera.title: Build a better soil blend
Monstera.summary: Mixing your own potting medium lets you tailor it to exactly what your plant needs.
Monstera.concept: A good all-purpose indoor mix combines standard potting soil for nutrients and water retention with perlite for drainage and aeration. Adding orchid bark creates a chunkier mix ideal for plants like Monsteras that prefer excellent drainage.
Monstera.keyTakeaway: Reward: Soil Blender badge — craft the perfect foundation for healthier roots.

quiz.prompt: What does adding perlite to a standard potting mix primarily improve?
options: Drainage and aeration around the roots

Basil.title: Chase kitchen-window sun
Basil.summary: Basil is happiest with strong daily light and steady moisture, especially on a bright sill.
Basil.concept: Basil grows fast when it gets several hours of sun. Weak light quickly leads to pale, stretched stems.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Sun Sipper badge — set up a productive herb corner.

quiz.prompt: What does basil want most from its starter setup?

Basil.title: Pinch above leaf pairs
Basil.summary: Small, frequent harvests make basil bushier and keep it from becoming a tall bare stick.
Basil.concept: Pinching top growth above a leaf pair encourages side shoots. That means more leaves to harvest and a fuller plant.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Bushy Builder badge — shape better kitchen harvests.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Regularly pinching basil tips can encourage bushier growth.

Basil.title: Catch flowers early
Basil.summary: Once basil focuses on flowers, leaf quality and flavor often drop off.
Basil.concept: Flowering shifts the plant toward reproduction. Removing flower buds early helps keep growth leafy for longer.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Flavor Keeper badge — extend the tasty stage.

quiz.prompt: You notice tiny flower buds forming on your basil, but you want more leaves for cooking. What is the best move?
options: Pinch off the buds and keep harvesting

Basil.title: Keep the soil evenly moist
Basil.summary: Basil dislikes the dramatic swing between bone-dry and soaked roots.
Basil.concept: Aim for lightly moist soil most of the time. Consistency helps basil stay tender and less stressed.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Harvest Rhythm badge — build a dependable care loop.

quiz.prompt: Which watering rhythm suits basil best?
options: Let it fully dry for many days
Flood it daily until water pools

Basil.title: Protect basil from cold
Basil.summary: Basil is one of the most cold-sensitive herbs you can grow indoors or out.
Basil.concept: Basil suffers at temperatures below 10°C and can be killed by frost overnight. Keep it away from cold drafts, air-conditioning vents, and outdoor temperatures in autumn and spring.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Warm Guardian badge — keep your basil in its comfort zone.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Basil can tolerate temperatures below 10°C for extended periods without damage.

Basil.title: Deal with aphids and whitefly
Basil.summary: Basil attracts common soft-bodied pests — catching them early keeps harvests clean.
Basil.concept: Aphids cluster on new growth and undersides of leaves; whiteflies rise in a cloud when you disturb the plant. A strong spray of water followed by insecticidal soap or neem oil handles most infestations without harsh chemicals near your food.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Herb Guard badge — keep pest pressure low on edible plants.

quiz.prompt: Which pest treatment is most appropriate for basil that you plan to eat?
options: Insecticidal soap or diluted neem oil spray
Letting the pests run their course

Basil.title: Size the container right
Basil.summary: A pot that is too small stunts basil, while one that is too large waterloggs the roots.
Basil.concept: A 15–20 cm pot is usually ideal for one basil plant. Good drainage holes are essential. If you grow multiple plants, give each its own space rather than crowding them together.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Pot Selector badge — match the container to the herb.

quiz.prompt: What pot size works best for a single basil plant?
options: About 15–20 cm with good drainage holes
The smallest pot you can find
A very large pot shared with several other herbs

Basil.title: Choose your basil variety
Basil.summary: Beyond classic sweet basil, a range of varieties suit different uses and tastes.
Basil.concept: Sweet basil is the most versatile for cooking. Thai basil has an anise flavour and holds up better to heat. Purple basil adds colour to salads. Lemon basil brightens fish and grain dishes. Each has slightly different care needs but the same core requirements.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Variety Explorer badge — match the basil variety to your kitchen style.

quiz.prompt: Which basil variety has an anise-like flavour and holds up better when cooked?

Basil.title: Store cut basil correctly
Basil.summary: Fresh basil stored correctly stays vibrant for days, not hours.
Basil.concept: Stand freshly cut stems in a glass of water at room temperature — never in the fridge, as cold turns leaves black. Change the water daily and keep the glass away from direct sun.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Freshness Keeper badge — get the most from every harvest.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Storing fresh basil in the refrigerator is the best way to keep it fresh.

Basil.title: Give basil rich, well-drained soil
Basil.summary: Basil does its best in fertile, loose soil that never sits wet.
Basil.concept: A good-quality potting mix enriched with a little compost gives basil the nutrients it needs. Avoid heavy or compacted soils — they hold too much water and reduce the air around the roots.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Rich Roots badge — start with the right foundation for strong growth.

quiz.prompt: What soil type suits basil best for container growing?
options: A quality potting mix with some compost added
Cactus mix with extra coarse sand

Basil.title: Root basil cuttings in water
Basil.summary: A spare stem from your existing plant can become a whole new plant in a week.
Basil.concept: Cut a non-flowering stem just below a leaf node, remove the lower leaves, and place it in a glass of clean water in bright indirect light. Roots usually appear within seven to ten days.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Water Rooter badge — multiply your herb supply for free.

quiz.prompt: True or false: A basil cutting placed in water in bright indirect light can develop roots within about a week.

Basil.title: Succession plant for continuous basil
Basil.summary: Sowing a new pot of basil every few weeks keeps the harvest going all season.
Basil.concept: Any single basil plant will eventually bolt and slow down. Starting fresh seeds or cuttings every three to four weeks means you always have a young, productive plant ready to take over when the previous one fades.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Continuous Harvest badge — never run out of fresh basil.

quiz.prompt: What does succession planting basil every few weeks achieve?
options: A continuous supply of young, productive plants

Basil.title: Plant basil near tomatoes
Basil.summary: Basil and tomatoes are classic garden companions with real practical benefits.
Basil.concept: Basil may help deter aphids and whiteflies from nearby tomato plants. The pairing also makes culinary sense — both prefer similar sun and warmth conditions, making them easy to manage together.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Companion Planner badge — use plant relationships to your advantage.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Basil and tomatoes share similar growing conditions and may help deter pests when grown together.

Basil.title: Save seeds from your best plant
Basil.summary: Letting one basil plant bolt to seed gives you free seeds for next season.
Basil.concept: Allow flower stalks to fully mature and dry on the plant. Once the seed pods turn brown and papery, pinch them off, let them dry indoors for a few more days, then crush and store the seeds in a cool dry place.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Seed Saver badge — close the loop from plant back to seed.

quiz.prompt: When should you harvest seeds from a basil plant?
options: After flower pods turn brown and dry on the plant
While flowers are still bright and fresh
As soon as the plant starts to bolt

Basil.title: Keep basil through winter
Basil.summary: Basil will not survive outdoors in winter, but a sunny indoor spot extends the season.
Basil.concept: Bring basil indoors before the first frost and place it on the brightest windowsill available. Supplement with a grow light if natural light is weak. Water carefully — winter indoor conditions are drier and less forgiving.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Winter Herb badge — extend your fresh basil season with smart placement.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Basil can survive outdoors through the winter in most temperate climates.

Basil.title: Why pinching makes herbs bushier
Basil.summary: Removing growing tips sounds counterintuitive, but it unlocks more growth.
Basil.concept: When you pinch the growing tip of an herb, the plant redirects energy to side shoots lower on the stem. Those side shoots become new branches, resulting in a fuller, more productive plant over time.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Pinch Pro badge — use one simple technique to double your yield.

quiz.prompt: What happens to an herb plant after you regularly pinch its growing tips?
options: It sends energy to side shoots and grows bushier

Basil.title: Running a kitchen herb garden
Basil.summary: A small collection of herbs near the kitchen is one of the most practical garden projects.
Basil.concept: Group herbs with similar care needs together. Water when the top of the soil feels dry. Harvest often to keep plants producing. Avoid overfertilizing — less-fertile conditions often produce more intensely flavoured herbs.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Kitchen Gardener badge — build a harvest-ready herb corner.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Overfertilizing herbs tends to reduce the intensity of their flavour.

Basil.title: Harvest herbs at the right moment
Basil.summary: The best flavour comes from harvesting before herbs enter the flowering phase.
Basil.concept: Most herbs have their peak flavour just before they begin to flower. For leafy herbs like basil, parsley, and mint, harvesting in the morning after any dew has dried gives the most aromatic leaves.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Peak Flavour badge — time your harvest for maximum taste.

quiz.prompt: When do most leafy herbs have the most intense flavour?
options: Just before flowering, harvested in the morning
After they have fully flowered and set seed
During the coldest weeks of winter

Basil.title: Dry herbs to preserve flavour
Basil.summary: Air-drying is simple and preserves most of the essential oils that make herbs valuable.
Basil.concept: Tie small bunches of stems together and hang them upside down in a warm, dry, well-ventilated space away from direct sunlight. Most herbs are fully dry within one to two weeks. Store in sealed glass jars.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Preservation Pro badge — extend your harvest beyond the growing season.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Drying herbs upside down in a warm, dry, ventilated space is an effective way to preserve them.

Basil.title: Feed herbs lightly and carefully
Basil.summary: Herbs need nutrients, but too much fertilizer changes their character.
Basil.concept: A half-strength balanced liquid fertilizer every three to four weeks during the growing season is sufficient for most potted herbs. Overfertilizing pushes soft, watery growth with reduced essential oil concentration.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Light Feeder badge — fertilize herbs for quality, not just quantity.

quiz.prompt: What effect does overfertilizing commonly have on culinary herbs?
options: Soft, watery growth with less intense flavour

Basil.title: Organic pest control for herbs
Basil.summary: Chemical pesticides and edible herbs do not mix well — natural alternatives work.
Basil.concept: Neem oil diluted in water and sprayed on affected plants handles most soft-bodied pests. Insecticidal soap works similarly. For small outbreaks, a strong stream of water from a hose or tap is often enough.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Clean Crop badge — keep edible plants free from harmful chemicals.

quiz.prompt: Which pest control approach is most appropriate for herbs you intend to eat?
options: Neem oil spray or insecticidal soap

Basil.title: Container drainage essentials
Basil.summary: Good drainage in pots prevents the most common herb-killing mistake.
Basil.concept: Always use pots with drainage holes. Avoid placing a solid saucer directly under — if water pools there, empty it after watering. A layer of gravel at the bottom of a pot does not improve drainage and is a myth worth dropping.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Container Wise badge — build the habit that protects every potted herb.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Placing gravel at the bottom of a pot significantly improves drainage for potted herbs.

Basil.title: Soil pH and plant health
Basil.summary: The acidity or alkalinity of your soil controls which nutrients plants can actually use.
Basil.concept: Most herbs and vegetables prefer a slightly acidic to neutral pH of around 6.0 to 7.0. Outside this range, nutrients become chemically locked and unavailable even if they are present in the soil. A basic pH test kit reveals your soil's status quickly.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: pH Checker badge — understand the invisible factor behind nutrient uptake.

quiz.prompt: What pH range do most herbs and vegetables prefer?
options: Slightly acidic to neutral — around 6.0 to 7.0

Basil.title: Use compost to enrich soil
Basil.summary: Compost is the simplest and most reliable soil improver you can add to any garden.
Basil.concept: Adding mature compost to potting mixes or garden beds improves drainage in clay soils, improves water retention in sandy soils, and feeds soil microbes that in turn release nutrients to plants. Even a small amount makes a meaningful difference.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Compost Convert badge — incorporate organic matter as a foundation habit.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Adding compost improves both water retention and drainage depending on the soil type it is added to.

Basil.title: Consistent watering prevents stress
Basil.summary: Wild swings between very wet and very dry stress plants more than either condition alone.
Basil.concept: Consistent moisture — watering at regular intervals and always checking the soil before adding more — reduces stress cycles. Stressed plants are weaker, more pest-prone, and produce less flavour in herbs or fruit in vegetables.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Steady Waterer badge — build a routine your plants can rely on.

quiz.prompt: Why does inconsistent watering — swinging between very wet and very dry — harm plants?
options: It creates stress cycles that weaken growth and reduce yield
It makes plants grow too fast
It has no measurable effect on plant health

Basil.title: Make the most of a south window
Basil.summary: A south-facing window is prime real estate for sun-loving herbs and vegetables.
Basil.concept: In the northern hemisphere, south-facing windows receive the most consistent sunlight throughout the day. Placing full-sun plants like basil, rosemary, and chillies there maximises their light exposure without supplemental grow lights.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Window Optimizer badge — use your best natural light spot wisely.

quiz.prompt: True or false: In the northern hemisphere, a south-facing window typically receives the most sun throughout the day.

Basil.title: Avoid waterlogged herb roots
Basil.summary: More basil, mint, and parsley die from overwatering than from any other single cause.
Basil.concept: Herbs in containers are especially vulnerable because water has nowhere to escape if the pot or saucer traps it. Always check soil moisture before adding more water, and never let pots sit in standing water for more than an hour.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Wet Stopper badge — protect tender herb roots from excess moisture.

quiz.prompt: Your basil leaves are yellowing and wilting even though you watered recently. The soil feels very wet. What should you do?
options: Stop watering and let the soil dry out — this looks like overwatering
Add fertilizer to revive the plant

Basil.title: Understand and prevent bolting
Basil.summary: Bolting sends plants into reproduction mode — understanding why it happens helps you prevent it.
Basil.concept: Bolting — sending up flower stalks rapidly — is triggered by long day lengths, heat, drought stress, or the plant detecting that its season is ending. For herbs, preventing or delaying bolting keeps leaves productive. Cool temperatures, consistent moisture, and regular harvesting all slow bolting.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Bolt Blocker badge — keep herbs in their productive leaf stage longer.

quiz.prompt: Which combination of conditions most commonly triggers bolting in leafy herbs?
options: Long days, heat stress, or drought
Regular harvesting and consistently good moisture

Basil.title: Neem oil for pest prevention
Basil.summary: Neem oil is one of the most versatile organic pest tools available to home gardeners.
Basil.concept: Neem oil disrupts the life cycle of many common garden pests, including aphids, spider mites, and fungus gnats, without harming beneficial insects when used correctly. Dilute it with water and a small amount of liquid soap, and spray in the evening to avoid leaf burn.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Natural Defender badge — add neem oil to your organic toolkit.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Neem oil should be sprayed in the evening rather than in direct sun to avoid burning leaves.

Basil.title: Match herbs to the season
Basil.summary: Some herbs love summer heat while others prefer cooler conditions — knowing which is which prevents frustration.
Basil.concept: Basil, chillies, and lemongrass are warm-season herbs that thrive in heat and die in frost. Parsley, coriander, and chives are cool-season herbs that bolt in summer heat. Growing each in its right season dramatically improves success rates.
Basil.keyTakeaway: Reward: Seasonal Planner badge — choose the right herb for the right time of year.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a cool-season herb that performs best outside of the hottest summer months?

Tomato.title: Support fruiting stems early
Tomato.summary: Tomatoes grow fast and benefit from cages or stakes before they get heavy.
Tomato.concept: Early support prevents stem damage, improves airflow, and makes later fruit load easier to manage.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Stem Saver badge — prepare for bigger growth.

quiz.prompt: What should you prioritize for a tomato starter?

Tomato.title: Water deeply, not constantly
Tomato.summary: Tomatoes do better with thorough watering sessions than with tiny splashes all day.
Tomato.concept: Deep watering encourages stronger root systems, while shallow frequent splashes often leave roots near the surface.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Root Runner badge — train deeper roots.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Deep, consistent watering is usually better for tomatoes than frequent tiny splashes.

Tomato.title: Feed the flowering plant
Tomato.summary: Tomatoes burn a lot of energy once they start pushing flowers and fruit.
Tomato.concept: Balanced feeding supports blooms, fruit set, and stronger stems. It does not replace sunlight or watering.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Bloom Booster badge — support the fruiting phase.

quiz.prompt: Your tomato has flowers forming, pale older leaves, and strong sun exposure. What care change helps most?

Tomato.title: Leave room for airflow
Tomato.summary: Crowded foliage traps humidity and makes tomato care harder as the plant thickens up.
Tomato.concept: Good spacing and airflow help reduce moisture-related disease pressure and keep leaves drying faster after watering.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Garden Coach badge — manage a more resilient plant.

quiz.prompt: Why does airflow matter around tomatoes?
options: It helps reduce moisture-related disease pressure

Tomato.title: Remove suckers for focused growth
Tomato.summary: Pinching out suckers keeps your tomato's energy directed where it matters most.
Tomato.concept: Suckers are shoots that sprout in the axil between the main stem and a leaf branch. Left unchecked on indeterminate varieties, they become full branches that dilute fruit size and quantity. Pinch them off when small — under 5 cm — with clean fingers.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Sucker Stopper badge — direct energy to bigger, better fruit.

quiz.prompt: Where do tomato suckers grow, and why should you remove them on indeterminate varieties?
options: Between the main stem and leaf branch — they take energy from fruit production
On the roots — they block water absorption
At the very top of the plant — they shade lower leaves

Tomato.title: Help tomato flowers set fruit
Tomato.summary: Tomatoes self-pollinate but sometimes need a little help indoors or in still-air gardens.
Tomato.concept: Tomato flowers release pollen when vibrated. Outdoors, wind and insects handle this. Indoors or in calm conditions, gently tapping or shaking the flower clusters daily during flowering helps pollen transfer and improves fruit set.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Pollination Helper badge — ensure every flower has the best chance to become fruit.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Gently shaking or tapping tomato flower clusters can help improve fruit set in low-wind or indoor conditions.

Tomato.title: Prevent tomato flower drop
Tomato.summary: Flowers falling off before setting fruit is frustrating — and usually preventable.
Tomato.concept: Blossom drop is most often caused by temperature extremes above 32°C or below 10°C at night, inconsistent watering, or nutrient imbalances. Keeping temperatures steady, watering consistently, and feeding with a balanced fertilizer during flowering dramatically reduces the problem.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Flower Fixer badge — keep every blossom on the path to fruit.

quiz.prompt: Your tomato flowers are dropping off before any fruit forms during a heatwave. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Temperature too high — provide shade cloth or move to a cooler spot
Too much fertilizer — flush the soil with water

Tomato.title: Prevent blossom end rot
Tomato.summary: That dark, sunken patch on the bottom of tomatoes is calcium deficiency in action.
Tomato.concept: Blossom end rot is not caused by a lack of calcium in the soil — it results from inconsistent watering that prevents the plant from moving available calcium to the developing fruit. Keeping soil moisture even is the most effective prevention.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Rot Preventer badge — protect the fruit you have worked hard to grow.

quiz.prompt: What is the most effective way to prevent blossom end rot in tomatoes?
options: Consistent watering to help the plant move calcium to fruit
Adding large amounts of calcium fertilizer
Moving the plant into full shade

Tomato.title: Mulch to keep moisture steady
Tomato.summary: A layer of mulch around your tomato plant is one of the most impactful low-effort improvements.
Tomato.concept: Mulch — straw, wood chip, or leaf litter — slows moisture evaporation from the soil surface, moderates soil temperature, and suppresses weeds. Apply a 5–8 cm layer around the base, keeping it clear of the stem to avoid rot.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Mulch Maker badge — reduce watering frequency while improving soil health.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Mulching around tomatoes reduces water evaporation and helps maintain more consistent soil moisture.

Tomato.title: Determinate vs indeterminate tomatoes
Tomato.summary: Choosing the right tomato type changes how you grow and harvest all season.
Tomato.concept: Determinate tomatoes (bush types) fruit all at once and stop growing at a set height — good for small spaces and one-time harvests. Indeterminate types keep growing and fruiting all season until frost, need more pruning, and reward ongoing care.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Tomato Type badge — pick the variety that matches your space and goals.

quiz.prompt: What is the key difference between determinate and indeterminate tomato varieties?
options: Determinate types set all fruit at once; indeterminate types keep fruiting all season
Determinate types are always larger and taller
Indeterminate types need no support or pruning

Tomato.title: Plant tomatoes deep for strong roots
Tomato.summary: Tomatoes are unusual in that burying the stem encourages new root growth along it.
Tomato.concept: Unlike most plants, tomatoes can develop roots along buried stem sections. Planting them up to their lowest leaves — or even deeper — produces a larger, more resilient root system that anchors the plant and improves drought tolerance.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Deep Planter badge — use deep planting to build a stronger root base.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Planting tomatoes deeply so that stem is buried can encourage additional root growth along the buried section.

Tomato.title: Spot common tomato diseases early
Tomato.summary: Catching blight or fungal issues early is the difference between a lost season and a saved one.
Tomato.concept: Early blight shows as dark spots with yellow rings on lower leaves. Late blight appears as water-soaked grey patches that spread quickly in wet conditions. Remove affected leaves immediately and avoid overhead watering to limit spread.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Disease Scout badge — inspect regularly and act fast.

quiz.prompt: What is the first step when you notice dark spots forming on lower tomato leaves?
options: Remove affected leaves immediately and stop overhead watering
Add more fertilizer to boost plant immunity
Increase watering frequency to dilute any disease

Tomato.title: Know when a tomato is truly ripe
Tomato.summary: Colour alone is not always enough — feel and smell also signal readiness.
Tomato.concept: A ripe tomato gives slightly when squeezed gently, detaches from the vine with little effort, and has a rich, earthy scent near the stem. Most tomatoes are best harvested when fully coloured but still firm — they continue to ripen off the vine in warm conditions.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Harvest Ready badge — pick tomatoes at the perfect moment.

quiz.prompt: A tomato is fully red but still feels very firm. What should you do?
options: Leave it a few more days and check again — it may still need time
Cut it open to check the inside right now

Tomato.title: Finish the tomato season well
Tomato.summary: How you end the season affects next year's success more than most gardeners realise.
Tomato.concept: Remove all plant material — including fallen fruit, leaves, and stems — from the bed at the end of the season to reduce overwintering disease spores. Avoid composting tomato material if disease was present. Adding compost to the bed now improves conditions for next year.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Season Closer badge — a clean finish sets up a strong start.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Removing all tomato plant material at the end of the season helps reduce disease carry-over to the following year.

Tomato.title: Pair tomatoes with companion plants
Tomato.summary: The right neighbours make tomato growing easier and more productive.
Tomato.concept: Basil may deter aphids and whiteflies. Marigolds planted around the bed repel nematodes and some insects. Carrots improve soil texture near tomato roots. Avoid planting tomatoes near fennel or brassicas — both can inhibit tomato growth.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Garden Neighbour badge — choose companions that earn their space.

quiz.prompt: Which plant is considered a beneficial companion for tomatoes?
options: Basil — may help deter aphids and whiteflies
Fennel — improves overall tomato root growth
Brassicas — provide shade and reduce water needs

Tomato.title: Vegetables need full sun
Tomato.summary: Most fruiting vegetables demand significantly more sun than foliage plants.
Tomato.concept: Tomatoes, peppers, courgettes, and beans all need at least six to eight hours of direct sunlight daily. Less than this sharply reduces fruit set and yield. Before placing a vegetable bed, track the sun across the site throughout the day.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Sun Planner badge — place vegetables where they will actually thrive.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Most fruiting vegetables like tomatoes and peppers need at least six to eight hours of direct sun each day.

Tomato.title: Watering a vegetable garden
Tomato.summary: Consistent moisture is one of the biggest factors separating a productive garden from a struggling one.
Tomato.concept: Most vegetables need about 2.5 cm of water per week, either from rain or irrigation. Deep watering two to three times a week is better than shallow daily watering. A drip line or soaker hose at soil level reduces leaf disease by keeping foliage dry.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Irrigation Pro badge — water at the root, not the leaf.

quiz.prompt: Which watering approach works best for reducing leaf disease in a vegetable garden?
options: Drip or soaker line at soil level
Overhead sprinkler applied twice a day
Hand watering leaves and soil together

Tomato.title: Fertilizing a vegetable garden
Tomato.summary: Vegetables are heavy feeders compared to most ornamental plants.
Tomato.concept: Start with compost-enriched soil. Once plants begin flowering or fruiting, switch to a fertilizer higher in phosphorus and potassium to support fruit development. Overapplying nitrogen after flowering pushes leafy growth at the expense of fruit.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Feed Strategist badge — time your inputs to match what plants need.

quiz.prompt: Your tomato plant has started flowering. Should you continue using a high-nitrogen fertilizer?
options: Switch to a fertilizer higher in phosphorus and potassium for better fruit development
Keep using high-nitrogen fertilizer for faster overall growth
Stop fertilizing entirely once flowering begins

Tomato.title: Manage garden pests naturally
Tomato.summary: Pest management works best when you prevent problems before they take hold.
Tomato.concept: Healthy plants grown in good soil resist pests better. Physical barriers, companion planting, and encouraging beneficial insects like ladybirds and lacewings provide lasting protection. Treat only when necessary and start with the gentlest effective method.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Balanced Garden badge — build a garden where problems stay manageable.

quiz.prompt: What is the first line of defense against garden pests?
options: Healthy soil and strong plants — they naturally resist pests better
Immediate application of pesticide at the first sign
Removing all plants that show any pest activity

Tomato.title: Harvest often to keep yield going
Tomato.summary: The more you harvest, the more most plants will produce.
Tomato.concept: Many vegetables — courgettes, beans, cucumbers, tomatoes — stop producing aggressively if overripe fruits are left on the plant. Harvesting regularly signals the plant to keep producing. A daily walk through the garden during peak season prevents missed harvests.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Regular Harvester badge — pick often to keep the production cycle going.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Leaving overripe vegetables on the plant can slow overall production.

Tomato.title: Succession planting extends the harvest
Tomato.summary: Staggering sowing dates gives you a longer season of fresh vegetables rather than a glut followed by nothing.
Tomato.concept: Instead of sowing all your seeds at once, plant small batches every two to three weeks. This spreads harvest times, reduces waste, and keeps your garden producing steadily across a longer window.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Succession Planner badge — turn one big harvest into many smaller, continuous ones.

quiz.prompt: What does sowing seeds in small batches every two to three weeks achieve?
options: A continuous, spread-out harvest instead of a single large glut
Faster germination for each individual batch
Larger individual vegetables from each plant

Tomato.title: Benefits of raised bed gardening
Tomato.summary: Raised beds solve many common garden problems in one go.
Tomato.concept: Raised beds drain better than in-ground beds, warm up faster in spring, and allow precise control over soil quality. They also reduce weeding and make it easier to manage pests. A depth of 30–40 cm suits most vegetables.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Raised Bed Builder badge — understand why raised beds consistently outperform bare ground.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Raised beds typically warm up faster in spring and drain better than flat in-ground garden beds.

Tomato.title: Improving garden soil
Tomato.summary: Most garden soils benefit from improvement before you start planting.
Tomato.concept: Clay soil drains poorly and compacts easily — adding compost and coarse sand helps. Sandy soil drains too fast and holds few nutrients — add compost and organic matter. Both soil types improve significantly with regular annual additions of compost.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Soil Improver badge — diagnose and fix your starting point before planting.

quiz.prompt: What amendment improves both clay and sandy soil types?
options: Compost — it improves structure and nutrient content in both
Fine gravel — it breaks up any heavy soil type
Chemical fertilizer — it compensates for poor soil structure

Tomato.title: Rotate crops to protect soil
Tomato.summary: Moving where you plant each vegetable family each year prevents problems from accumulating.
Tomato.concept: Growing the same crop family in the same spot every year builds up soil-borne diseases and pest populations that target that family. A simple four-year rotation — nightshades, brassicas, legumes, roots — breaks problem cycles and improves long-term soil health.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Rotation Planner badge — build a habit that pays off over many seasons.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Rotating vegetable families through different beds each year can help reduce soil-borne disease build-up.

Tomato.title: Core organic gardening principles
Tomato.summary: Organic gardening is less about avoiding chemicals and more about building a healthy system.
Tomato.concept: Building healthy soil through compost and organic matter, encouraging natural pest predators, and choosing disease-resistant varieties are the core strategies. This approach is slower to set up but produces a more resilient and self-sustaining garden over time.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Organic Mindset badge — grow with the system, not against it.

quiz.prompt: What is the foundation of a sustainable organic garden?
options: Building healthy soil through compost and organic matter
Using only water and sunlight without any amendments

Tomato.title: How plants use nutrients
Tomato.summary: Understanding what plants actually eat helps you feed them more intelligently.
Tomato.concept: Plants absorb nutrients dissolved in water through their roots. Nitrogen supports green growth. Phosphorus powers roots and flowering. Potassium builds resilience and fruit quality. Micronutrients like iron, magnesium, and calcium play supporting roles that become obvious when they are missing.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Nutrition Expert badge — feed plants based on what they actually need.

quiz.prompt: Which nutrient primarily supports strong roots and flower formation in plants?

Tomato.title: Why mulch helps every garden
Tomato.summary: Mulch is one of the highest-return, lowest-effort improvements you can make to any garden.
Tomato.concept: Mulch suppresses weeds by blocking light, retains soil moisture, moderates soil temperature, and — if organic — breaks down over time to improve soil structure. Apply 5–10 cm around plants, keeping it away from stems to prevent rot.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Mulch Master badge — adopt mulching as a consistent garden practice.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Mulch helps gardens by suppressing weeds, retaining moisture, and moderating soil temperature simultaneously.

Tomato.title: Setting up efficient watering
Tomato.summary: A simple irrigation system saves time, reduces disease, and grows better vegetables.
Tomato.concept: Drip irrigation delivers water directly to the root zone, reducing evaporation and keeping foliage dry. A timer eliminates guesswork and ensures consistency even when you are busy or away. Starting with just a few drip lines for your most demanding crops gives immediate returns.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Irrigation Installer badge — set up water delivery where plants need it most.

quiz.prompt: What is the main advantage of drip irrigation over overhead watering?
options: It delivers water to the root zone while keeping foliage dry
It uses significantly more water overall
It only works well for tall plants

Tomato.title: Growing vegetables in containers
Tomato.summary: Containers let you grow food in almost any space, from a balcony to a kitchen step.
Tomato.concept: Choose the largest container practical for the vegetable — tomatoes need at least 40 litres, lettuce can thrive in 10 litres. Use a high-quality potting mix, water more frequently than in-ground beds, and fertilize regularly as nutrients leach out faster with frequent watering.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Container Grower badge — produce food in any space with the right setup.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Container-grown vegetables typically need watering and fertilizing more frequently than in-ground crops.

Tomato.title: Wrapping up the growing season
Tomato.summary: What you do at the end of the season determines how easy next year will be.
Tomato.concept: Clear spent plants promptly to reduce overwintering pests and disease. Add a thick layer of compost to beds and let it rest through winter. Plant cover crops like mustard or clover if you want to protect and improve soil structure before spring.
Tomato.keyTakeaway: Reward: Season Wrapper badge — set your garden up for next year before you close it down.

quiz.prompt: What is the main benefit of adding compost to vegetable beds at the end of the season?
options: It improves soil structure and nutrient content over winter ready for spring planting
It immediately feeds any plants still in the ground
It prevents all weeds from growing the following year
